hints: Compare the positions of calcium (Group 2) and cobalt (first row transition metal) and recall how atomic mass and atomic size change between them.
Think about what density depends on, mass per unit volume, and how heavier atoms packed into a smaller volume affects this.
Think about metallic bonding strength, how many electrons each atom contributes to the sea of delocalised electrons and the charge on the cation.
walkthrough:
Picture the two metals side by side**
Calcium is a Group 2 s-block metal with $A_r$ about 40. Cobalt is a first row d-block metal with $A_r$ about 59. Cobalt atoms are also smaller because across the period nuclear charge increases and the 3d electrons shield poorly, pulling the outer electrons in closer.

Link mass and packing to density**
Density is mass divided by volume. Cobalt gives you more mass per atom and packs those atoms into a smaller atomic volume, so mass per unit volume is much greater. That is why transition metals feel heavy for their size compared to s-block metals like calcium.

Link delocalised electrons to melting point**
Melting breaks metallic bonds, the attraction between positive cations and the sea of delocalised electrons. Calcium contributes its two 4s electrons. Cobalt contributes its 4s electrons plus 3d electrons, so there are more delocalised electrons per atom and a higher cation charge. The attraction is stronger, so more thermal energy is needed to break it and melting point is higher.

Final answer: Density of cobalt is higher than calcium. Melting point of cobalt is higher than calcium.
Density higher because Co has larger $A_r$ and smaller atomic radius, so heavier atoms packed more closely.
Melting point higher because Co has stronger metallic bonding due to greater number of delocalised electrons and stronger attraction between cations and sea of electrons.

hints: Focus on the two essential components that must be present, the centre and what surrounds it.
walkthrough:
Build the picture of a complex**
Imagine a central $\text{Co}^{3+}$ ion acting as a host. Around it sit small molecules or ions like $\text{NH}_3$ or $\text{Cl}^-$ called ligands. They use a lone pair to bond to the metal. That whole assembly of central metal plus attached ligands is the complex, which may be a cation, anion or neutral molecule.
Final answer: A central transition metal atom or ion surrounded by one or more ligands.

hints: Recall what must stay the same and what must change for any isomers, then apply it to which atoms are inside versus outside the brackets.
walkthrough:
Separate formula from structure**
Both $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]\text{SO}_4$ and $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]\text{Br}$ contain Co, $5\text{N}$, $15\text{H}$, Br, S and $4\text{O}$. The atom count is identical. What differs is connectivity, in one $\text{Br}^-$ is bonded to Co and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is free, in the other it is reversed. Same atoms, different structural formula means structural isomers.
Final answer: Compounds with the same number and type of atoms but different structural formulae, different arrangement of bonds.

hints: Count the ligands bonded directly to Co in $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]^{2+}$ to get the coordination number and the expected shape.
walkthrough:
Count then shape**
There are five $\text{NH}_3$ plus one $\text{Br}$ bonded to Co, so coordination number is 6. Six groups around a centre repel to give an octahedral arrangement with $90^{\circ}$ bond angles.

Draw in 3D**
Put Co in the centre. Draw four ligands in a square plane with straight lines, one $\text{NH}_3$ on a solid wedge coming toward you and $\text{Br}$ (or the sixth $\text{NH}_3$) on a hashed wedge going away from you. Label ligands clearly and add the $2+$ charge outside the brackets. That wedge and dash convention shows the octahedron in three dimensions.

Final answer: Shape is octahedral. 3D diagram shows central Co with five $\text{NH}_3$ and one $\text{Br}$ arranged octahedrally, using solid wedges for bonds coming out, hashed wedges for bonds going back, and straight lines for bonds in plane.

hints: Think about where both electrons in the Co to N bond come from.
walkthrough:
Follow the electron pair**
Nitrogen in $\text{NH}_3$ has a lone pair. Cobalt(III) has vacant 3d and 4s orbitals to accept it. When $\text{N}$ donates both shared electrons to Co, that is the definition of a co-ordinate or dative covalent bond, not a normal covalent bond where each atom supplies one electron.
Final answer: Co-ordinate (dative covalent) bond.

hints: Assign charges of $\text{NH}_3$ as 0, $\text{Br}$ as -1 and $\text{SO}_4$ as -2, then balance against the overall ion charge to find Co.
walkthrough:
Balance charges to find Co**
Let oxidation number of Co be $x$. For $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]^{2+}$: $$x + 5(0) + (-1) = +2$$ so $x = +3$. For $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]^+$: $$x + 5(0) + (-2) = +1$$ so $x = +3$. Both contain cobalt(III). $\text{NH}_3$ is neutral so it never changes the sum.
Final answer: In $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]^{2+}$ oxidation number of Co = +3. In $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]^+$ oxidation number of Co = +3.

hints: Remember only the ion outside the brackets is free in solution and will give a precipitate, the coordinated ion is locked to Co and does not react.
Recall the two classic precipitation tests, acidified $\text{AgNO}_3$ for halides and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ for sulfates, and their precipitate colours.
walkthrough:
Spot what is free**
These are ionisation isomers. In $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]\text{SO}_4(aq)$ the $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is free and $\text{Br}^-$ is coordinated. In $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]\text{Br}(aq)$ the $\text{Br}^-$ is free and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ is coordinated. Only free ions react in the tests.

Test for free bromide**
Add dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ to remove interfering ions, then $\text{AgNO}_3(aq)$. Free $\text{Br}^-(aq) + \text{Ag}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgBr}(s)$ gives a cream precipitate. So $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]\text{Br}$ gives cream precipitate, the other gives no reaction.

Test for free sulfate**
Add $\text{BaCl}_2(aq)$ or $\text{Ba}(\text{NO}_3)_2(aq)$. Free $\text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) + \text{Ba}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s)$ gives a white precipitate. So $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]\text{SO}_4$ gives white precipitate, the other gives no reaction.

Final answer: Test 1: add dilute $\text{HNO}_3$ then $\text{AgNO}_3(aq)$ / $\text{Ag}^+(aq)$. $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]\text{Br}$ gives cream precipitate of $\text{AgBr}$, $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]\text{SO}_4$ gives no precipitate.
Test 2: add $\text{BaCl}_2(aq)$ / $\text{Ba}(\text{NO}_3)_2(aq)$ / $\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)$. $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Br}]\text{SO}_4$ gives white precipitate of $\text{BaSO}_4$, $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{SO}_4]\text{Br}$ gives no precipitate.

hints: Think about what causes colour in transition metal complexes, the splitting of d-orbitals and promotion of a d electron.
Consider how changing a ligand from $\text{Br}^-$ to $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ changes the size of that splitting and therefore the light absorbed.
walkthrough:
Recall where colour comes from**
Colour is not the ligands themselves. Ligands split the 3d orbitals into two sets of different energy. White light shines on the complex, a d electron absorbs a photon with energy equal to the gap, $\Delta E = h\nu$, and jumps to the higher set. The colour you see is the rest of the light that is not absorbed.

Change ligand, change gap, change colour**
$\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ are different ligands with different field strengths, so they split the d-orbitals by a different amount. A different $\Delta E$ means a different frequency and wavelength is absorbed. Absorbing different parts of the spectrum leaves different complementary colours to be seen, so the two isomers look different.

Final answer: Different ligands cause different splitting of d-orbitals, so d-d energy gap $\Delta E$ is different.
Different wavelength / frequency of visible light is absorbed to promote a d electron, so different complementary colour is transmitted / observed.

hints: Recall the simple phase rule, same physical state as reactants means homogeneous, different physical state means heterogeneous.
Check each example, solids like Fe and $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ with gaseous reactants versus ions and gases all mixed in the same phase.
walkthrough:
Apply the phase test**
If catalyst and reactants are in the same phase it is homogeneous, if in different phases it is heterogeneous. This is the only test you need.

Sort the four cases**
Haber: $\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g)$ with solid $\text{Fe}(s)$, different phases, so heterogeneous. $\text{I}^-(aq) / \text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}(aq)$ with $\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq)$, all aqueous, so homogeneous. $\text{SO}_2(g)$ oxidation catalysed by $\text{NO}_2(g)$, both gases, so homogeneous. Contact: $\text{SO}_2(g)$ oxidation with solid $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5(s)$, different phases, so heterogeneous.

Final answer: Fe in the Haber process: heterogeneous. $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ in the $\text{I}^-/\text{S}_2\text{O}_8^{2-}$ reaction: homogeneous.
$\text{NO}_2$ in the oxidation of $\text{SO}_2$: homogeneous. $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ in the Contact process: heterogeneous.
